newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Peres says Netanyahu risks rewarding bombers.
newsitem.headline: Peres says Netanyahu risks rewarding bombers.

text.p: Former Israeli prime minister Shimon Peres warned his successor Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday that security crackdowns on Palestinians for a double suicide bombing in Jerusalem risked handing victory to the bombers.

Peres said Netanyahu, who ousted him in knife-edge elections last year after a wave of similar attacks on Israelis, was weakening Palestinian authorities at the same time as he told them to take tough action against the militant Hamas movement.
"I think one has to be very careful not to allow Hamas emerge as the winners of this action, particularly as they are the ones who did it," Peres told Reuters in an interview.

Israel imposed a closure on the West Bank and Gaza after last Wednesday's attack which killed 15 people, including two bombers. It has also withheld customs revenues due to the Palestinians, arrested 156 suspected militants and threatened to re-enter Palestinian areas to flush out more.

Peres, a Nobel peace laureate and an architect of the historic 1993 interim peace deal with the Palestine Liberation Organisation, said he was "alarmed" at the months of deadlock in Middle East talks.
He said the region would return to "a chaotic situation" if Netanyahu's government let the accord fall apart.

"The government of Israel can hold back the peace process but if this is the case anti-peace forces will accelerate their acts," said Peres, succeeded by former army chief Ehud Barak as leader of the main opposition Labout party two months ago.

Israeli-Palestinian talks had already been stalled for months over Netanyahu's expansion of Jewish settlements when the bombers struck. Statements in the name of Hamas claimed responsiblity for the bombings and warned of more attacks.

A wave of Hamas bombings last year which killed scores of Israelis helped turn Israeli electors away from Peres towards Netanyahu, who promised greater security and a tougher line in talks with Palestinians.
Netanyahu has accused Arafat of doing "damn all" to fight militants and warned that peace talks were in danger unless he took more action.
But Peres said accusations by government officials that Palestinian officials had been fomenting violence were exaggerated.

"The Palestinian Authority should cooperate with us in fighting terrorism. But on the other hand we have to permit them to do so by not crushing them to a point where they become incapable of action," he said.
"You can look at Arafat as you want, as a partner or as an enemy, but you cannot paint him as a puppet."

Peres, who also closed off the Palestinian territories after anti-Israeli attacks when he was prime minister, said the closures should be limited because of their dramatic impact on the Palestinian economy.
But he said withholding customs revenue was "ridiculous" and a violation of the peace deal.
Unless the peace process made significant progress, Peres said, Israel would once again be isolated in the Middle East, facing a renewed arms race, an Arab boycott and military threats.
"I think if there won't be a full renewal of the peace momentum we will enter a dangerous period. I don't want to sound alarmist, but I am alarmed."
